2609.20005.title: Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models
2609.20005.paper_summary: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.
2609.20005.paper_summary_zh: 人們越來越多地轉向 AI 聊天機器人以獲取新聞和世界事件的解釋。<lb/>但當他們用不同語言提問時，是否會獲得相同的政治答案？<lb/>在這裡，我們展示了問題的語言如何改變相同 AI 系統對烏克蘭戰爭的評估。<lb/>我們請 GPT、Claude 和 Gemini 評估關於戰爭的二十個陳述，使用 112 種語言，收集了 67,200 個回應。<lb/>親俄和親烏的回應在不同語言中存在差異。<lb/>當我們按國家的官方語言對回應進行分組時，它們遵循一種類似於全球政治分歧的模式：相對較多的親俄回答對應於對俄羅斯的較有利的公共觀點、在聯合國投票中對烏克蘭的支持較少，以及對烏克蘭的援助較少。<lb/>這一廣泛模式在所有三個模型中重現，並且在移除個別陳述對時仍然存在。<lb/>我們的發現表明，信息戰爭可能通過影響用於訓練 AI 模型的文本，進而傳播地緣政治偏見。
2609.20005.author: Maxim Chupilkin et.al.
